meta.title: How HTTPS keeps your connection private
meta.source_label: Source: How HTTPS keeps your connection private

beats.say: Is the padlock in your browser really protecting you?
Here's the problem. Anyone on the path could read plain HTTP traffic.
cite: could read or change plain HTTP traffic

beats.say: The fix is HTTPS. It wraps HTTP in TLS for encryption, integrity, and authentication.
cite: HTTPS fixes this by wrapping HTTP inside TLS.

beats.say: Every connection starts with a handshake. The server sends its certificate.
cite: The server replies with its choice and its certificate.

beats.say: Your browser checks that certificate. A wrong name triggers a warning.
cite: If the signature does not verify, or the name does not match the site, the browser shows a warning.

beats.say: Both sides agree on a shared secret, with fresh keys each session.
cite: TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, so each session gets fresh keys.

beats.say: And it's quick. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip.
cite: TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in one round trip

beats.say: Even if a server key leaks later, past sessions stay protected.
cite: Even if a server key leaks later, past sessions stay protected.
Automation tools renew them without human effort.

beats.say: The padlock protects the path between you and the server, nothing more.
cite: It protects the path between you and the server, nothing more.

beats.say: Next time you see that padlock, which handshake step will you picture first?

cards.title: Certificate
cards.body: A signed statement that a public key belongs to a domain. The browser warns if it does not verify.

cards.body: Even if a server key leaks later, past sessions stay protected.
